Moreover, corrections such as these appear not only in the isolated context of estimating entropy, but also become relevant when estimating e.g. discrete mutual information. results.title: Analyzing and Bootstrapping Our Way to a Better Entropy Estimator — Part II, Computational — thirdorderscientist
results.content: Since we're dealing with a discrete distribution, \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}\) essentially gives us \(\hat{F}\) (after a few cumulative sums), and we're all set to generate our bootstrap estimates of the bias of \(\hat{H}\). We then compute the entropy estimate for each bootstrap sample, call these \(\hat{H}^{b}\). For bootstrapping, we don't know \(\mathbf{p}\), so we sample the \(\hat{H}^{b}\) using \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}\) instead, and get \[ \widehat{\text{Bias}}(\hat{H}) = E\_{\hat{p}}[\hat{H}] - H(\mathbf{\hat{p}}) \approx \frac{1}{B} \sum\_{b = 1}^{B} \hat{H}^{b} - H(\hat{\mathbf{p}})\] as our bias estimate. Since we want the bias to be zero, we subtract this off from our estimator, giving a new estimator \[ \hat{H}\_{\text{bootstrap}} = \hat{H} - \left(\frac{1}{B} \sum\_{b = 1}^{B} \hat{H}^{b} - H(\hat{\mathbf{p}})\right) = 2 \hat{H} - \frac{1}{B} \sum\_{b = 1}^{B} \hat{H}^{b}.\] And thus, with a great deal of computing going on in the background, we have a new way to estimate entropy. The histogram in the top panel is the estimated distribution using the bootstrap samples \(\{ \hat{H}^{b}\}\_{b = 1}^{B}\).

results.content:
Title: Sebastian Nowozin's slow blog – Estimating Discrete Entropy, Part 2
# Estimating Discrete Entropy, Part 2. In 1955 George Miller proposed a simple correction to the naive plugin estimator \(\hat{H}\_N\) by adding the constant offset in the bias expression as follows. This is an improvement over the plugin estimator but the added offset does not depend on the distribution but only on the sample size. ### Jackknife Estimator. In a nutshell, jackknife resampling methods are used to estimate bias and variance of estimators. The use of jackknife bias estimation to improve entropy estimation was suggested by (Zahl, 1977). The jackknife bias-corrected estimator of the plugin estimator is given as follows. The quantity \(\hat{H}^{(\cdot)}\_N\) is the average of \(n\) estimates obtained by leaving out a single observation. Interestingly, normally it would be expensive to compute \(n\) leave-one-out estimates. Here however, two tricks are possible: First, because the histogram is a sufficient statistic, we need to compute only \(K\) holdout estimates instead of \(n\). Second, one can interleave computation in such a way that computing each holdout estimate is \(O(1)\), reducing the overall computation of \((\ref{H:jackknife})\) to \(O(K)\) runtime and no additional memory over the plugin estimate. In essence, the computational complexity is comparable to that of the inexpensive plugin estimate, making the jackknife estimator computationally cheap. ### Grassberger Estimator. Another proposal for an improved estimator is due to Peter Grassberger. where the logarithm of the original naive estimator \(\hat{H}\_N\) have been replaced by a scalar function \(G\), defined as. (The function \(G(h)\) is the solution of \(G(h)=\psi(h)+(-1)^h \int^1\_0 \frac{x^{h-1}}{x+1} \textrm{d}x\) given as equation \((30)\) in the paper.) Computationally this estimator is almost as efficient as the original plugin estimator, because for integer arguments the digamma function can be accurately approximated by an efficient series expansion. We obtain \(n=100\) samples from the distribution and estimate the entropy based on this sample. * The Plugin estimator fares badly on both RMSE and bias;. * The Miller estimator fares less badly, suggesting RMSE is affected mainly by bias, however, significant errors remain for small values of \(\alpha\);. * The Bayes estimator fares almost as bad as the plugin estimator, except for \(\alpha=1/2\). * The Jackknife, Grassberger 2003, and NSB estimators provide excellent performance throughout the whole range of \(\alpha\) values.

results.title: [E] What makes exact distribution of an estimator hard to calculate? : r/statistics
results.content: [E] What makes exact distribution of an estimator hard to calculate? Skip to main content[E] What makes exact distribution of an estimator hard to calculate? [E] What makes exact distribution of an estimator hard to calculate? We have heard in class that exact distribution of estimator(statistic) is hard to calculate, therefore, many times we resort to asymptotic distribution of a statistic usually derived from MLE. Good unbiased estimators, in general, are conditioned on a sufficient statistic which may be some complicated function of f(X1,... Most estimators can be expressed in some ways as sums of independent or even dependent random variables, and the CLT is an easy way to compute the distribution of those estimators. > the CLT is an easy way to ~~compute~~**approximate** the distribution of those estimators. An asymptotic approximation is certainly not equal to the _exact_ distribution of an estimator, which is what the OP was asking about. By definition, any estimator of a parameter is a function of some sufficient statistic. The Rao-Blackwell theorem the OP mentioned allows one to transform any estimator into another estimator whose MSE is no larger than the first one, by conditioning on a sufficient statistic. It is the only generally applicable procedure for constructing more efficient estimators, but as the OP said the computation of the conditional distribution may be intractable. > We have heard in class that exact distribution of estimator(statistic) is hard to calculate,. In other cases, it's not as simple as that; you often have estimators that are not available in closed form but are instead obtained by iterative solutions of equations (e.g. attempting to identify where the derivative of a log-likelihood goes to 0), or more generally by iterative optimization methods (e.g. findinf the argument, θ that minimizes -log L(θ) where L is the likelihood and θ is your parameter-vector). If your estimator involves a sum or average of random variables, you can sometimes use _numerical convolution_ to compute small sample distributions; for example I've used Fast Fourier Transforms to get to a prediction interval for a sum of future values (predictions), where the distributions of the components of the sum was tractable but the distribution of the sum itself was not.
